prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Trailing her father, bearing his hand axe, the girl thought she had never guessed what earthly majesty was before then, as he strode unconcernedly holding a vicious gander by the horny mitts and let the big wings batter his knees. She was also surprised to feel a liberating satisfaction in the coming bloodshed, and that notwithstanding all the times she had been beleaguered and had fled, today she did not fear the barnyard hubub. Yet, as her father’s clever stroke fell, as the pronged head skipped sideways and the neck plumes stiffened with blood from the cleft, she was angry; and, when the headless goose ran to the brook and was carried off into the woods alive, she rejoiced, and subsequently frequented those woods and avoided her father. When the goose began to mend she brought him small hominy, which was welcome though she had to press the kernels one by one into the pink neck that throbbed into her palm; when haemorrhage occurred she would not spare handkerchiefs, and stanching the spot she felt a thrill of sympathy. But for the most part there was steady progress, and growing vigor was accompanied by restlessness, and one cool day the blind thing was batted out of existence by a motorcycle. She had no time for tears. She ran upstairs to miss her father’s barytone commiseration, then out onto the fields, and, holding an old red pinwheel, ran ran ran ran.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Through a girl’s shifting response to her father’s attempted slaughter of a vicious gander, the narrative explores violence, compassion, and estrangement as she secretly nurses the wounded bird back to health. When the recovering goose is abruptly killed by a motorcycle, her wordless flight reveals both the fragility of her redemptive bond and her deepened alienation from her father’s world.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Trailing, She, Yet

outputs.L1:
Trailing her father and carrying his hand axe, the girl thought she had never before understood earthly majesty: he strode unconcernedly along, gripping a vicious gander by its horny mitts and letting its great wings batter his knees. She was surprised, too, by the liberating satisfaction she felt at the prospect of bloodshed, and by the fact that, despite all the times she had been beleaguered and had fled, she did not fear the barnyard hubbub that day.

Yet, as her father’s deft stroke fell, as the pronged head glanced sideways and the neck plumes stiffened with blood from the cleft, she grew angry. And when the headless goose ran to the brook and was carried alive into the woods, she rejoiced. Thereafter, she frequented those woods and avoided her father.

When the goose began to mend, she brought him small hominy, which he welcomed, though she had to press the kernels one by one into the pink neck throbbing against her palm. When hemorrhaging occurred, she did not spare her handkerchiefs, and as she stanched the wound, she felt a thrill of sympathy. For the most part, however, his recovery progressed steadily, and his growing vigor was accompanied by restlessness. Then, one cool day, the blind creature was batted out of existence by a motorcycle.

She had no time for tears. She ran upstairs to avoid her father’s baritone commiseration, then fled into the fields and, clutching an old red pinwheel, ran ran ran ran.
outputs.L2:
The girl followed behind her father with his small axe, awed by a grandeur she had never known could exist in the world. He walked calmly ahead, gripping a savage gander by its tough feet while its broad wings pounded against his knees. To her surprise, the prospect of violence brought a freeing sense of pleasure. Although the bird had cornered and chased her many times before, the uproar in the yard no longer frightened her that day.

But when her father brought down the axe with practiced skill—when the forked head glanced aside and blood hardened the feathers around the split neck—her exhilaration turned to anger. After the decapitated goose fled toward the stream and was swept, still living, into the forest, she felt glad. From then on, she often visited those woods and kept away from her father.

As the goose began recovering, she fed it bits of hominy. The food was gratefully received, though she had to push each grain separately into the exposed pink neck as it pulsed against her hand. Whenever the wound started bleeding again, she freely sacrificed her handkerchiefs to stop it, experiencing a sharp surge of compassion as she pressed them to the injury. Most of the time, however, the bird improved steadily. Its returning strength also made it increasingly restless.

Then, on a chilly day, a motorcycle struck the blind creature and killed it. There was no opportunity for her to cry. She hurried upstairs to avoid hearing her father’s deep-voiced condolences, then rushed outside across the fields. Clutching an old red pinwheel, she ran and ran and ran and ran.
outputs.L3:
At first, the girl admires her father’s commanding presence and is surprised to find that the prospect of the gander’s slaughter neither frightens nor disturbs her. Instead, she feels strangely calm and satisfied. However, when her father strikes the bird, her feelings change abruptly. She becomes angry with him and secretly rejoices when the wounded, headless gander escapes into the woods.

Afterward, the girl avoids her father and searches for the bird. Once she finds it, she secretly cares for it, feeding it hominy and trying to stop its bleeding. Under her care, the gander gradually recovers its strength. Despite surviving the initial attack, however, it is eventually struck and killed by a motorcycle.

Unable to face either her grief or the sympathy she expects from her father, the girl runs away from him. Carrying a red pinwheel, she races through the fields, using movement and distraction to avoid confronting the pain of the gander’s death.
outputs.L4:
At first, the girl accepts her father’s determination to kill the vicious gander as a necessary response to the bird’s aggression. Yet when the slaughter goes wrong and the badly injured goose survives, her attitude changes. Faced with its pain and helplessness, she can no longer see it merely as a dangerous animal. Without telling her father, she hides the wounded bird and begins caring for it, bringing it food, tending its injuries, and patiently helping it regain its strength. What begins as pity gradually becomes a private bond and an act of resistance against the harshness of her father’s world.

As the gander recovers, the girl invests its survival with redemptive meaning. Saving the bird allows her to answer violence with compassion and to preserve something her father had tried to destroy. At the same time, her secrecy widens the emotional distance between them: she cannot share her tenderness with him because she senses that he would neither understand nor respect it. The recovering goose thus becomes both her companion and the symbol of an inner life increasingly separate from her father’s values.

That hope is shattered when the gander, newly restored to health, is suddenly struck and killed by a motorcycle. The death is abrupt and senseless, undoing all the girl’s patient care in an instant. Overcome by grief, she does not explain herself or seek comfort from her father. Instead, she runs away in silence. Her flight expresses more than sorrow for the bird; it reveals her loss of faith in the possibility that compassion can protect what she loves. It also confirms her estrangement from her father and from a world governed by brutality, accident, and emotional incomprehension. Through the girl’s changing response to the gander—from fear, to pity, to devotion, and finally to grief—the narrative presents tenderness as both a moral awakening and a source of painful isolation.
outputs.L5: She walked ahead without looking back, her shadow trailing across the empty road. The sun had already disappeared, yet the horizon still held a thin line of gold. Somewhere beyond it waited a life she had not imagined—but was finally ready to claim.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal Southern Gothic short scene about a girl who helps her father behead a vicious goose, secretly nurses the headless bird back to health, and then loses it in a motorcycle accident. End with her running through fields holding a red pinwheel.
counterfactuals.output:
The goose had bitten three deacons, a mule, and the county tax assessor before Daddy decided the Lord had withdrawn His favor.

At sundown he carried it to the chopping stump behind the smokehouse. The bird bucked under my hands, white wings beating the dusk into flour. Its eyes were black and furious, old as nails.

“Hold tight, Lulabelle.”

Daddy raised the hatchet. The sun balanced on its edge.

Afterward, he took the head away in a feed sack, meaning to nail it over the henhouse as a warning. The body he left twitching among the pokeweed.

But near midnight I heard scratching beneath my window.

The goose stood in the yard without its head.

A pale knob of neck swayed above its shoulders, neatly sealed as if stitched by moonlight. It tapped one webbed foot, impatient.

I hid it in the abandoned baptismal shed beyond the creek. Every morning before school, I brought cracked corn, rainwater, and spoonfuls of cane syrup. I whispered lessons into the small red throat-hole: the names of saints, the multiplication tables, the lies Mama told before she vanished. The goose listened with its whole body.

Soon it grew strong. It learned to drink through a silver funnel. It slept with its wings folded like a widow’s hands. Though it had no mouth, I sometimes heard it honk from far inside itself, the sound traveling up from the earth beneath us.

By August it could follow my motorcycle down the clay roads, running beside me in a white blur. Daddy thought the feathers on my dresses came from angels.

Then, one Sunday, a storm rose black over the cotton fields. The goose chased me past the cemetery, wings spread, neck-stump pointed toward heaven. Rain turned the road to red grease.

I never saw the washed-out bridge.

The motorcycle went sideways. I flew into the ditch. The goose struck the rear wheel and vanished beneath a thunder of feathers.

When I woke, the storm had passed. The motorcycle smoldered upside down. White feathers clung to the telephone wires for miles, trembling though there was no wind.

I searched until winter. I searched the creek, the briars, the dry wells, and the dreams of every sleeping dog in the county. Sometimes, at night, something headless scratched beneath my window. But when I looked, there was only moonlight and the soft red mud.

In spring, Daddy found the goose’s skull inside the feed sack, singing.

I stole it before dawn and buried it under the chopping stump. Then I took the red pinwheel from the grave of a child I had never known and ran through the fields, holding it high while it spun and spun, pointing everywhere the lost go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single dense literary paragraph exploring a child’s conflicting feelings toward violence, sympathy, and her father after a botched barnyard slaughter.
counterfactuals.output: After her father’s first blow glanced from the lamb’s skull and sent it staggering sideways into the trough, the girl felt horror rise in her like a scream, yet beneath it, shamefully, a bright needle of excitement, because the yard had broken open into something truer than chores and weather, something adults kept hidden behind clean plates and folded grace; then the lamb found its feet and stood trembling, blood stippling its white face, and all grandeur vanished into pity so fierce she hated the world for permitting pain and hated her father for bringing it down with his own hand, though she saw, too, how his mouth tightened, how he whispered, “Easy now,” as if gentleness might still enter what he had begun. When the second blow failed, she wanted him stopped, wanted him stronger, wanted to run to the animal and wanted not to touch it, and in the terrible pause before he lifted the hammer again she understood that mercy could wear the same raised arm as cruelty, that love might make a person clumsy rather than kind, and that her father—huge in his stained apron, blinking hard against the flies—was neither the monster she needed nor the protector she remembered, but only a frightened man finishing badly what he believed had to be done; afterward, when he washed his hands at the pump and would not look at her, she longed to put her arms around him almost as much as she longed never to forgive him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Tell a darkly comic, emotionally unsettling story in elevated, old-fashioned prose about a girl who initially welcomes a gander’s execution but later rescues and cares for the decapitated animal.
counterfactuals.output:
### The Widow’s Gander

In the village of Bellweather there lived a gander so abominable that even the parson, who maintained that all creatures were footnotes in the Book of Providence, confessed he could not discover the moral purpose of that bird.

His name was Solomon.

He possessed a white body of great dignity, a yellow eye of judicial severity, and a disposition such as might have disgraced a tax collector. He bit the washerwomen upon their calves, overturned the sexton’s luncheon, and once pursued the apothecary through an open grave, into which that learned gentleman descended with more haste than reverence. Children went abroad armed with switches. Dogs crossed the lane when they saw him coming.

None hated Solomon more faithfully than Miss Honoria Vane, aged eleven.

He had torn the blue ribbon from her Easter bonnet; he had consumed her arithmetic; and, upon one memorable afternoon, had driven her three times round the village pump while the blacksmith laughed until he became ill. Honoria thereafter spoke of the gander’s death with a composure beyond her years.

“I hope,” she said, “they make a pie of him large enough for the whole parish.”

Thus, when her aunt announced that Solomon must be dispatched for Michaelmas, Honoria received the intelligence as a patriot might receive news of victory.

At dawn she attended the execution.

The yard was silvered with frost. Solomon stood upon the chopping block with his feet bound and his neck stretched forward, looking less like a criminal than a bishop inconvenienced by ceremony. Widow Vane held him; Mr. Crumb, the butcher, held the axe.

“Would you care to say farewell?” asked the widow.

“I hope he understands every moment of it,” said Honoria.

The axe fell.

Solomon’s head landed in a basket with an expression of profound disapproval.

His body, however, rejected the verdict.

It leapt from Widow Vane’s hands, ran beneath the butcher’s apron, overturned the pail, struck the yard gate, and vanished into the cabbage field.

Mr. Crumb swore. Widow Vane fainted. Honoria laughed so violently that she had to cling to the block.

But laughter, like milk, may turn without warning.

That evening, while the village searched for Solomon’s fugitive carcass, Honoria heard a soft knocking at the kitchen door.

There stood the gander’s body.

It swayed faintly upon its webbed feet. Its severed neck had been stoppered by a clumsy clot of black blood and cabbage leaves. It gave no cry, naturally, but tapped its beakless breast against the door with dreadful patience.

Honoria’s first thought was to scream.

Her second was that Solomon had returned specifically for her.

Her third—small, shameful, and somehow worse than fear—was that he looked cold.

She smuggled him into the coal shed.

For three days she fed him by pushing soaked bread into the neck with a silver teaspoon. Most of it came out again. Some appeared to remain. Solomon slept standing beneath her old cloak, his headless neck tucked beneath a wing by habit, which was an affecting sight and also a ridiculous one.

Honoria wept the first time she saw him do it.

“This does not mean I forgive you,” she whispered.

The gander shifted his feet.

“Nor that you forgive me.”

He shifted them again.

By the week’s end he could navigate the shed without colliding with the scuttle. He seemed to perceive Honoria by some faculty not dependent upon eyes. When she entered, his wings lifted. When she left, he followed, striking walls and furniture with a melancholy perseverance.

The villagers, meanwhile, assumed a fox had taken him. Mr. Crumb declared that headless poultry often ran some distance, though he grew evasive when asked whether it commonly opened latches.

Winter came.

Honoria lined a bonnet box with wool and made Solomon a collar from mourning crape. He became gentler in death than he had ever been in life. He no longer bit, though this improvement had been mechanically assisted. He sat beside her while she practised scales. He followed her to the privy. Once, during family prayers, he entered the parlour and stood behind Widow Vane like an accusation.

The widow turned, saw him, and screamed, “Lord preserve us!”

At this, Solomon spread his wings and knocked over the tea service.

After a long silence, Honoria said, “He is much improved.”

The widow attempted to burn him.

Honoria carried him into the woods beneath her cloak, though he was heavy and dripped upon her stockings. They hid in an abandoned keeper’s cottage. There she tended him with bread mash, linseed, and the desperate ingenuity of love.

For it was love now, though of an ugly species.

She loved him not because he was harmless, nor because he was pitiable, but because she had wished him dead and death had proved insufficient. Each day he remained seemed both a rebuke and a pardon. His terrible absence of a face relieved her of the need to know which.

In spring, rumours spread of a ghostly bird wandering the churchyard. Old Mrs. Fen claimed it had chased her husband’s spirit from the alehouse. The parson preached upon the resurrection of the flesh, then amended his sermon to clarify that this was not ordinarily expected before Judgment.

Honoria grew pale. Solomon grew thin.

One April morning she found him motionless beside her bed of primroses. His wings were folded. His feet, which had walked so stubbornly beyond their proper term, were curled beneath him.

She sat for a long while in the wet grass.

“You horrid thing,” she said at last. “You might have told me.”

She buried him beneath the pear tree, placing his body in the grave first. Then, after some consideration, she fetched the basket from the icehouse, where his head had been kept for soup and subsequently forgotten.

It had shrivelled somewhat, but retained its expression.

Honoria laid it beside the body, not upon it.

“You were never very good at being whole,” she said.

That autumn the pear tree bore fruit shaped like little white birds. No one would eat them. Widow Vane had the tree cut down, but its stump continued to bloom every Michaelmas.

Years afterward, when Honoria had become a stern and charitable lady, she kept geese upon her estate. They were notorious creatures. They ruined gardens, attacked visitors, and hissed during funerals.

Whenever the steward suggested the axe, Miss Vane fixed him with a yellow, almost judicial eye.

“No,” she said. “One must be careful what one makes headless. It may become attached to you.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid experimental fiction passage featuring a hand axe, a headless goose escaping into the woods, kernels of hominy fed into its severed neck, and the repeated closing phrase “ran ran ran ran.”
counterfactuals.output:
The hand axe stood in the stump as if the stump had grown an iron tongue.

Morning shivered silver over the yard. A basin flashed. Feathers turned in the mud like small surrendered flags. Then the goose—headless, astonished, impossible—rose from the block and beat its wings against the world.

It crossed the fence without seeing the fence.

It crossed the creek without hearing the creek.

It entered the woods, where every tree leaned back to let it pass, ran ran ran ran.

Grandmother gathered her apron and followed. In one pocket she carried kernels of hominy, white and swollen as old teeth. In the other, a spool of red thread. She left the hand axe buried in the stump, its handle trembling from what it had done.

The goose moved among beeches and black pines. Its severed neck opened and closed like the mouth of a crimson flower. No cry came out, yet the woods filled with honking: from roots, from mushrooms, from the dark wells beneath stones. The sound seemed to remember the missing head and call it home.

At dusk Grandmother found the goose circling a lightning-struck oak. It had worn a ring in the leaves. It had written one word with its feet, over and over, though nobody could read it.

She knelt. “Hungry?”

Into the hollow neck she fed three kernels of hominy.

The first fell into yesterday.

The second fell into winter.

The third struck something deep inside the goose that rang like a little bell.

The bird stiffened. The oak opened an eye in its bark. Far back in the yard, the hand axe tore itself free of the stump and dropped blade-first into the earth.

Grandmother fed the goose another kernel, and another. With each one, a feather lifted from the ground and fastened itself to the dark. Soon the sky was winged. Soon the stars were only holes punched through a vast white body.

Still the goose would not die properly.

Still it would not live.

It spun once around Grandmother, scattering leaves, and plunged deeper between the trees. She followed until her apron snagged on thorns and the red thread unspooled behind her, stitching trunk to trunk, wound to wound, world to world.

By midnight there was no yard. No stump. No basin. Only the woods swallowing their own paths, and the pale kernels shining where they had spilled, and ahead—always ahead—the soft percussion of webbed feet:

ran ran ran ran.

Grandmother called to it with the voice of the missing head.

The darkness answered in feathers.

And the goose ran ran ran ran.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a grotesque coming-of-age vignette in which a young girl follows her imposing father to kill a goose, becomes alienated from him when the bird survives, nurses it in secret, and flees rather than hear his consolation after its accidental death.
counterfactuals.output:
Her father went ahead with the hatchet tucked through his belt, its iron head bumping his thigh. He was so broad that the path seemed to close behind him. Nettles leaned away from his boots. Low branches combed his shoulders and sprang back trembling.

Mara followed with the grain sack.

Inside it, the goose made a sound like an old woman clearing her throat. Its body was hot against Mara’s ribs. One wing worked loose and beat blindly at her elbow.

“Hold it tight,” her father said.

She tightened her arms.

At the chopping block, the yard smelled of rain, feathers, and the sweet rot beneath the coop. Her father drew the goose out by its legs. It unfolded upside down, enormous and filthy-white, its long neck writhing toward the earth. Its black eye found Mara and fixed upon her with a bright, beadlike accusation.

Her father laid the neck across the block.

“Watch,” he said. “You eat, you ought to know.”

He raised the hatchet. For an instant he looked taller than the shed, taller than the poplars, a man built to blot out whatever he stood before.

The blade came down.

The goose tore free.

There was a spray of red, but not the clean red fan her father had promised. The hatchet had only bitten the side of the neck. The bird ran crookedly across the yard, wings striking buckets and fence posts, its head dangling at an impossible angle. It knocked over the washbasin and vanished beneath the brambles.

Her father swore. He searched with the hatchet in one hand and a lantern in the other until dusk made his face float above his body. He called the goose “finished” and “fox meat.” At supper, he chewed onions loudly and did not look at Mara.

Something had changed in him. Or perhaps something had failed to change. His hands were still huge. His voice still rattled the spoons. Yet Mara had seen the hatchet glance aside. She had seen death refuse him.

That night she crept to the brambles.

The goose was there, breathing wetly. Its neck had folded into the weeds like a broken hose. When Mara reached in, it struck her wrist with its beak, weak but vicious.

“Good,” she whispered. “Do that.”

She wrapped it in her nightdress and carried it to the abandoned privy behind the orchard. For eleven days she fed it mash stolen from the kitchen and water sweetened with honey. She cleaned the wound with strips torn from her petticoat. Yellow pus gathered under the feathers; flies stitched their eggs along the scab. The smell became warm and personal, almost human.

The goose survived.

Its neck healed twisted, so that its head sat low against its breast. It could not honk properly. Instead it produced a small, rusty gasp. Mara named it Mercy, though the bird showed none. It bit her fingers, fouled her shoes, and watched her with its hard black eye.

Her father noticed the missing grain.

“Rats,” Mara said.

He studied her. His face, usually simple as a closed door, seemed then to contain many rooms. But he only nodded.

Mara began to think of Mercy as proof—not of kindness, exactly, but of a crack in the world. A thing marked for death might crawl through. A father might be wrong. A girl might know something and keep it alive without permission.

Then, on the twelfth morning, she found the privy door open.

Mercy had dragged herself into the orchard. Beneath the pear tree lay the overturned water trough, one iron leg buried in the mud. The goose’s body protruded from under it, white feathers spread like dirty washing. Its crooked neck had been pinned flat.

Mara pulled until her nails split, but the trough would not move. She called the goose’s name. Once, absurdly, she hissed at it. The black eye remained open, filled with a tiny reflection of the sky.

Behind her, branches cracked under heavy steps.

Her father came into the orchard. He saw the mash bowl, the bloodstiff rags, the dead bird. His face changed—not to anger, which Mara could have borne, but to sorrow.

“Oh, girl,” he said softly.

He reached for her.

Mara understood that he meant to gather her against his vast chest. He meant to tell her accidents happened, that creatures died, that she had done all she could. He would make the world round and whole again with his deep voice. He would forgive her secrecy and perhaps ask her to forgive the hatchet.

She could not bear it.

Before his hand touched her, she ran.

She ran through the orchard, over the stone wall, and into the wet fields. Briars opened her shins. Mud sucked off one shoe. Behind her, her father called her name—not loudly, not in anger, which made it worse.

She ran until his voice became only another bird crying somewhere beyond the hedges.

Then she ran farther.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
